notes.meaning: Amos sees the Lord standing by the altar and giving the order to strike the building so hard that the ceiling collapses on the worshippers. God Himself directs this strike, showing that the place they trusted for worship cannot protect them from His judgment. Those who try to run away will still be caught and killed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the altar and shrine represent the corrupt religious system of northern Israel rather than a single literal building.

notes.meaning: Sinners will find no hiding place from God, even if they dig down into the grave or climb into the highest skies. God rules over the deepest depths and the highest heights, so His hand can pull anyone out of hiding. Human strength can never outrun divine justice.

Even if the people hide in the thick woods and caves of Mount Carmel, God will track them down. If they dive to the bottom of the sea, He will order the sea monster to strike them there. All of creation answers to the Lord, leaving no safe corner for those running from Him.

Surrendering to the enemy and marching into captivity will not guarantee safety either, because the sword will still reach them. The Lord warns that His watchful eye is set on them to bring harm instead of blessing. His promised curses for breaking the covenant will fully overtake them.

The Lord of Hosts shows His supreme power over the whole earth. A mere touch of His finger makes the ground tremble and melt, causing all its people to grieve. The land heaves and sinks like the rising and falling waters of the Nile River.

God builds His royal rooms high in the heavens and sets the dome of the sky firmly over the earth. He calls the ocean waters up into the clouds and pours them out across the land. The Lord is His name, reminding everyone that the Creator rules every part of the universe.

The Lord reminds Israel that their heritage gives them no special pass to sin. He guided other nations too, moving the Philistines from Crete and the Arameans from Kir, just as He led Israel out of Egypt. Relying on past blessings will not protect people whose hearts have turned away from God.

God keeps His eyes on the corrupt kingdom and plans to wipe it out as a political nation. At the same time, He promises not to destroy the whole family of Jacob completely. A remnant, meaning a small surviving group, will be preserved by His mercy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the promise to spare a remnant at the end of the verse was added later by a Judean scribe.

notes.meaning: The Lord compares the exile to shaking grain through a sieve among the nations. The violent shaking scatters the people, but not a single true grain will be lost. God carefully protects every faithful person while letting the worthless chaff fall away.

The unrepentant sinners among the people will fall by the sword. These are the arrogant people who claimed that trouble would never touch them or overtake them. False confidence cannot shield anyone from God's true warnings.

God promises a future day when He will rebuild David's fallen tent and repair all its broken walls. The royal family had sunk low like a battered shelter, but the Lord will restore it to honor. This points to the coming of the Messiah, Jesus, who restores God's kingdom.

differ.view: This promise is fulfilled spiritually in Jesus Christ and the gathering of believers into the church.
This foretells a future, literal restoration of David's kingdom over national Israel during an earthly reign of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars conclude that verses 11–15 were written after 586 BC because they describe David's dynasty as already fallen into ruins.

notes.meaning: God's restored people will take in what remains of old enemies like Edom and all the nations called by God's name. In Acts 15, the early church recognized that this scripture was being fulfilled as Gentiles, or non-Jewish people, turned to the Lord. God's kingdom expands to welcome people from every background.

A season of supernatural plenty is coming, where the harvest will be so huge that the plowman catches up to the reaper. The grape harvest will last until it is time to sow seed again, and the hills will seem to flow with sweet wine. This pictures the rich spiritual and material blessings of God's renewed world.

The Lord promises to bring His people back from their captivity and heal their land. They will rebuild their destroyed towns, live safely in them, plant vineyards, and drink their own wine. God reverses earlier curses and lets His people enjoy the fruit of their work.

God promises to plant His people firmly in their own soil, never to be torn away again. The Lord Himself guarantees this lasting peace and safety. His deep commitment to His people gives them hope that goes beyond all temporary trials.

differ.view: The promise of never being uprooted is fulfilled spiritually in the church, from which true believers can never be cast out.
This promise requires a future, permanent physical return of the Jewish people to the land of Israel that has not yet been fully realized.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Many popular teachers connect this promise directly to the establishment of the modern State of Israel in 1948 as the permanent fulfillment of the text.
